Finally, these load shapes were forecasted for future years using various state reports such as IEPR, Energy Efficiency Potential and Goals Study, and the SB100 report’s PATHWAYS model. Some limitations related to use of this cluster data should be noted. Firstly, the cluster load shapes were developed from 2020-2022, based on 2019 data and largely using 2021 state forecast reports. Therefore, more recent technology, policy, and adoption trends are not reflected in this data. Additionally, the end use cluster loads are aggregations of individual load estimates at best, and single representations of an estimated aggregated profile at other times. For example, the pool pump profile used in this study comes from the CEC ADM report, with the same profile being used to disaggregate pool pump loads in every customer cluster, subject to adjustments based on the total measured meter data in the cluster. This means that we cannot capture the full variability of end use loads, and therefore price response behaviors, across the customer base. 2.2 Dynamic price profiles 2.2.1 Dynamic price design Dynamic price profiles based on the CalFUSE concept have been developed for 2019 for prior studies (Gerke et al. 2022). Universal prices (one price profile per IOU, applicable to all 11 The three major IOUs in California are Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (SCE), and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E) 7 customer types) were originally developed, and later an adjustment methodology was added to ensure revenue neutrality to the average load shape of each customer class (Gerke et al. 2022; addendum). Additional price scenarios are developed for this study, along with forecasted prices to 2030. All price scenarios have several features in common; such that each profile is: ● Specific to a given IOU and customer class, such that the total revenue for the class average load shape is equal to the revenue of that load shape on the otherwise applicable tariff (i.e., the prevailing present day TOU tariff) ● Fully volumetric, with all revenues recovered via an hourly per-kWh price (no fixed costs or demand charges) ● Symmetric, such that the hourly price represents the cost to import as well as the revenue from exporting As described in Gerke et al. (2022), the hourly dynamic rate was determined by distributing the following categories of utility costs across the hours of the year: ● Wholesale electricity prices, encompassing both energy delivered to the consumer and line losses incurred during the delivery process, ● Generation capacity costs, including both traditional capacity and flexible capacity resources, ● Distribution system capacity costs, associated with energy delivery infrastructure, and ● Other costs, including transmission system infrastructure costs, account administration expenses, public-purpose programs, wildfire mitigation efforts, and other miscellaneous areas.
